Ukraine dismantles crypto scam network that stole €4.3 million

Ukrainian and German authorities arrested four people accused of running cryptocurrency investment scam call centers that stole more than €4.3 million from 135 German victims. The suspects allegedly used romance-baiting social engineering to funnel victims’ funds through crypto exchanges, bank accounts, and transit wallets.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Ukrainian law enforcement, working with German authorities, arrested four suspects accused of operating cryptocurrency investment scam call centers that stole more than €4.3 million.
  • 02The alleged scheme targeted 135 victims in Germany, using phone calls and messaging apps to persuade them to transfer funds into fraudulent cryptocurrency, share, and other investment platforms.
  • 03Police said the suspects helped victims open cryptocurrency exchange accounts, buy digital assets, and send them to accounts controlled by the criminal organization; in some cases, they also accessed victims’ online banking accounts.
  • 04Searches in the Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia, and Ivano-Frankivsk regions led to the seizure of cash, hardware cryptocurrency wallets, phones, SIM cards, computers, and other evidence.
  • 05The four suspects are in pre-trial detention and could face up to 12 years in prison if convicted of fraud and involvement in a criminal organization.

Ukrainian law enforcement, working with German authorities, arrested four suspects accused of operating cryptocurrency investment scam call centers. The alleged network stole more than €4.3 million from 135 victims in Germany. Those arrested include the alleged leader and three accomplices, and they are being held in pre-trial detention.

Police said the suspects used phone calls and messaging apps to build trust and persuade victims to invest in cryptocurrency, shares, and other financial instruments through fraudulent online trading platforms. They allegedly helped victims create cryptocurrency-exchange accounts, purchase digital assets, and transfer them to accounts controlled by the group; in some cases, they also accessed victims’ online banking accounts. The proceeds were allegedly moved through bank accounts, cryptocurrency exchanges, and transit wallets before being converted and distributed.

Searches conducted in August and September across the Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zaporizhzhia, and Ivano-Frankivsk regions resulted in the seizure of more than $90,000, nearly 600,000 Ukrainian Hryvnia, hardware cryptocurrency wallets, phones, SIM cards, and computer equipment. If convicted, the suspects could face up to 12 years in prison on charges related to fraud and participation in a criminal organization. The case follows other recent actions against fraudulent call-center networks operating in Ukraine that targeted people in Europe.

  • The alleged fraud did not rely only on convincing victims to send money directly; suspects reportedly guided them through opening cryptocurrency exchange accounts and buying digital assets, making the transactions appear like legitimate investing.
  • In some cases, the group allegedly obtained access to victims’ online banking accounts, indicating that the harm could extend beyond the money victims knowingly transferred into the fake investment platforms.
  • The alleged proceeds were moved through bank accounts, cryptocurrency exchanges, and transit wallets before being converted and distributed, showing that the operation used several channels to handle stolen funds.
  • The case involved authorities in Ukraine and Germany, while the searches occurred across four Ukrainian regions, illustrating the cross-border and geographically distributed nature of the alleged operation.

Ukrainian police, working with German authorities, arrested four people accused of running fake investment call centers that stole more than €4.3 million from 135 people in Germany. The group allegedly gained victims’ trust through phone calls and messages, then persuaded them to buy cryptocurrency or other investments on websites that were controlled by the scammers. This matters because similar scams can target people across Europe through dating sites, social media, and messaging apps, causing major personal financial losses.

France blames Iranian hackers for supermarket attacks that sparked fires

France has attributed October cyberattacks that disrupted refrigeration systems at roughly 700 retail locations, caused major food losses, and sparked at least 15 fires to the Iranian IRGC-linked Shahid Kaveh unit. The government plans to summon Iran’s ambassador and seek EU sanctions over the campaign.
KEY POINTS
  • 01France attributed October cyberattacks on refrigeration systems at approximately 700 retail locations to Shahid Kaveh, an Iranian IRGC-affiliated cyber-offensive unit.
  • 02Attackers remotely changed refrigeration controller defrost settings to high temperatures, leading to food losses, material damage, and at least 15 fires.
  • 03Affected organizations included Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour, Intermarché, smaller butcher shops, a slaughterhouse, and cooperative food-processing facilities.
  • 04French investigators also linked reconnaissance and attacks involving Schneider Electric industrial equipment at small hydroelectric installations to the same campaign.
  • 05France plans to summon Iran’s ambassador and seek new European Union sanctions against Iranian people and organizations involved in malicious cyber operations.

France has attributed October cyberattacks on refrigeration systems at roughly 700 retail and food-sector locations to Shahid Kaveh, an Iranian IRGC-affiliated cyber-offensive unit. The attacks occurred overnight on October 11–12, when attackers compromised refrigeration controllers and changed defrost settings to high temperatures. Affected organizations included major supermarket chains, smaller butcher shops, a slaughterhouse, and cooperative food-processing facilities. France said the disruption caused tens of millions of euros in food losses, material damage, and at least 15 fires.

France’s CERT-FR linked the activity to Shahid Kaveh through attacker infrastructure, reconnaissance of Schneider Electric industrial systems, use of the FOFA device-search platform, Farsi-language traces, and CyberbanNews posts publicizing the attacks. Investigators also connected attacks on Schneider Electric equipment at small hydroelectric installations to the same campaign, although the reported effects there were moderate. France attributed only the October attacks on French supermarkets to the Iranian unit, not later refrigeration incidents reported elsewhere in Europe. The French government said it will summon Iran’s ambassador and seek additional EU sanctions against Iranian individuals and organizations involved in malicious cyber operations.

  • The reported manipulation of defrost settings demonstrates that changing a single operational setting in refrigeration equipment can produce physical consequences, including fires, rather than only disrupting business operations.
  • France’s attribution relied on several overlapping indicators, including infrastructure used against Schneider Electric systems, use of FOFA, Farsi-language traces, and promotion of the incidents by the CyberbanNews outlet.
  • French authorities attributed only the October incidents in France to Shahid Kaveh, explicitly not extending that attribution to the later refrigeration attacks reported elsewhere in Europe.
  • The same campaign reportedly involved both food refrigeration equipment and small hydroelectric installations, indicating that its targets included multiple kinds of industrial equipment.

France says an Iranian government-linked hacking unit changed refrigerator settings at about 700 supermarkets, food businesses, and other locations in October. The disruption spoiled fresh and frozen food, caused tens of millions of euros in losses, damaged equipment, and was linked to at least 15 fires. Similar activity also affected small hydroelectric sites and blood-product storage facilities, showing that attacks on everyday equipment can create physical safety risks as well as financial damage.

France has publicly attributed a high-impact cyber operation against hundreds of food-sector sites to the Iranian IRGC-linked Shahid Kaveh unit, with physical consequences including fires and major losses. It is particularly relevant to organizations operating industrial refrigeration, cold-chain monitoring, and Schneider Electric industrial equipment.

Binance denies data breach after alleged ShinyHunters claims

Binance says it found no evidence that its systems or customer data were breached after an actor claiming to be ShinyHunters offered alleged records of 335 million users for sale. The exchange says the listing is likely a scam or may involve data stolen from users’ devices by infostealer malware rather than Binance systems.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A threat actor using the ShinyHunters name claimed to be selling records of 335 million Binance users for $900,000.
  • 02The alleged data included identity-verification documents, account passwords, cryptocurrency wallet private keys, transaction histories, email addresses, phone numbers, and internal infrastructure information.
  • 03Binance said it found no evidence that its systems, customer identity-verification data, credentials, wallet private keys, or internal infrastructure were compromised in connection with the listing.
  • 04Binance said similar listings have often involved information-stealing software that collected data from users’ own devices rather than a compromise of Binance systems.
  • 05Binance advised customers not to share passwords, two-factor authentication codes, seed phrases, or private keys and to remain alert for phishing attempts.

A threat actor using the ShinyHunters name claimed to be selling records allegedly belonging to 335 million Binance users for $900,000. The purported data included identity-verification documents, account passwords, wallet private keys, transaction histories, email addresses, phone numbers, and internal infrastructure information. The seller said Binance had two options: pay or have the data leaked. Binance said it found no evidence that the listed information came from a compromise of its systems.

Binance said it does not hold private keys for users’ external wallets, does not store passwords in plain text, and no longer operates in some jurisdictions referenced by the seller. The exchange said similar listings have often involved information-stealing malware that collects data from users’ own devices rather than a compromise of Binance itself. It advised users not to share passwords, two-factor authentication codes, seed phrases, or private keys and to remain alert to phishing attempts. The claim follows Binance’s confirmation that a separate fake job interview led an employee to install malware, which the company said enabled the theft of about $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency after wallet infrastructure was compromised.

  • Several details in the seller’s claim conflict with Binance’s stated practices: it does not hold private keys for users’ external wallets, does not store passwords in plain text, and no longer operates in some jurisdictions named in the post.
  • The article notes that similar alleged data sales can originate from information-stealing software on users’ personal devices, meaning exposed account information would not necessarily demonstrate that Binance itself was compromised.
  • Other forum users challenged the claim’s logic, asking why someone who possessed wallet private keys would sell them rather than use them directly.
  • The denial follows Binance’s confirmation that a separate fake-job-interview malware incident led to the theft of about $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency after wallet infrastructure was compromised.

Someone using the name ShinyHunters claimed to be selling information on 335 million Binance users for $900,000, including identity-verification documents, emails, phone numbers, passwords, and cryptocurrency wallet keys. Binance says it found no proof that its systems were broken into and believes the claim may be a scam or data taken from individual users’ devices. The claim still matters because if such information were real, criminals could use it to impersonate users, steal accounts, or take cryptocurrency; Binance advises users not to share passwords, two-step verification codes, recovery phrases, or wallet keys.

The article covers a specific, high-profile alleged data sale involving Binance and 335 million purported user records, although Binance says it found no evidence of a breach. It is relevant for monitoring credential theft, phishing risk, and threat-actor claims, but the core allegation remains unverified.

York University breach exposed personal information dating to 2007

York University disclosed that an attacker accessed personal data submitted through departmental web forms between 2007 and 2026, potentially exposing sensitive information including contact details, government IDs, health data, and financial information. The university is notifying those whose government ID or financial data was affected and offering two years of identity-protection services.

  • 01York University discovered on October 25 that an unauthorized actor had accessed limited online forms used by university departments.

  • 03The accessed information varied by person and included contact details, dates of birth, York ID numbers, government ID information, health information, academic and employment history, financial status, criminal background, demographic details, and images.
  • 04York University said the affected forms are now secure and will directly notify people whose government ID or financial account information was exposed, offering them two years of credit monitoring and identity theft protection.

York University in Toronto disclosed that an unauthorized actor accessed limited online forms used by university departments. The incident was discovered on October 25 and involved forms submitted across 14 university websites between 2007 and 2026. York said it acted to contain the incident after discovering it and that the forms are now secure and safe to use.

The stolen information varied by person and may have included email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, York ID numbers, government ID information, health information, academic and employment history, financial status, criminal background, demographic information, and images. York said most records contained basic contact information and York ID numbers, while the combination of contact data and other sensitive information can raise the risk of phishing and social-engineering attempts. The university will directly notify people whose government ID or financial account information was exposed and offer them two years of credit monitoring and identity theft protection.

York has not said how many individuals were affected or identified the perpetrators. Individuals who are not notified may contact the university to determine which types of their information were exposed. At the time of reporting, no ransomware group had publicly claimed responsibility for the incident.

  • Although York said most stolen records contained basic contact details and York ID numbers, some forms also held highly sensitive information such as government IDs, health information, financial status, and criminal background.
  • York explicitly noted that combining contact information with other exposed personal details increases the risk of convincing phishing and social-engineering scams.
  • Only people whose government ID or financial account information was exposed will be directly notified and offered two years of credit monitoring and identity theft protection; others must contact the university to learn what data of theirs was involved.

York University in Toronto says someone gained access to online forms used by university departments and took personal information submitted from 2007 through 2026. Hackers exploit SSHole OpenSSH flaw to breach Linux systems

Attackers are actively exploiting the SSHole flaw (CVE-2026-123158) in OpenSSH on certain musl-based Linux systems to bypass password-disabled accounts, steal credentials, and establish persistence. Administrators should upgrade to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or later and investigate anomalous password logins, SSH keys, and TAC Agent-related artifacts.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Attackers are actively exploiting SSHole, tracked as CVE-2026-123158, to execute commands, steal credentials, and maintain access on affected Linux systems.
  • 02SSHole affects certain musl-based Linux systems, including Alpine Linux, by allowing oversized passwords to bypass login restrictions for accounts whose password field is set to an asterisk.
  • 03OpenSSH fixed the vulnerability in version 10.6p2 on November 5, and public exploit code became available about four hours later.
  • 04GreyNoise observed successful attacks that performed system and container checks, queried cloud metadata services, attempted to obtain password hashes and root SSH keys, and modified authorized_keys files.
  • 05Administrators are advised to update OpenSSH, disable SSH password authentication on affected systems, and check for unexpected password logins, unauthorized SSH keys, and TAC Agent files or startup services.

Hackers are actively exploiting SSHole, tracked as CVE-2026-123158, to run commands, steal credentials, and establish continued access on affected Linux systems. The flaw affects certain musl-based systems, including Alpine Linux, and lets an attacker log in to accounts intended to be blocked from password sign-ins. Exploitation attempts began on November 5, when proof-of-concept code became available, and successful exploitation was recorded the following day. OpenSSH fixed the issue in version 10.6p2, released on November 5.

An oversized password can cause musl’s password-hashing function to return an asterisk on error, which OpenSSH incorrectly accepts as matching an account password field set to an asterisk. GreyNoise observed attackers conducting system and container reconnaissance, querying cloud metadata services, attempting to access password hashes and root SSH keys, and changing authorized_keys files for persistent access. In one case, an attacker gained root privileges and installed TAC Agent, although it could not contact its command-and-control server. Administrators are advised to update OpenSSH or disable SSH password authentication on affected systems, and to look for unexpected successful password logins, unauthorized SSH keys, and TAC Agent files or startup services.

  • Successful exploitation was recorded about 40 hours after the OpenSSH fix was released, showing that attacks began very soon after public exploit code became available.
  • The flaw does not affect accounts with valid password hashes and requires particular authentication settings, limiting exposure to specific configurations rather than every OpenSSH installation.
  • Although TAC Agent has no built-in mechanism to survive a restart, attackers attempted to compensate by creating a startup service.
  • One observed TAC Agent installation could not contact its command server and therefore never received a task, despite the attacker having gained root privileges.

Hackers are already using a flaw called SSHole in OpenSSH, a common tool for remotely accessing Linux computers, to get into certain systems without a working password. It affects some lightweight Linux setups, including Alpine Linux, where accounts were meant to have password sign-ins disabled. Once inside, attackers have tried to steal passwords and access keys, gain administrator control, and leave behind access so they can return later. Organizations using affected systems should update OpenSSH promptly or turn off password-based remote sign-ins.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is an active in-the-wild exploitation event affecting OpenSSH on certain musl-based Linux systems, with attackers observed stealing credentials, seeking root access, and attempting persistence. Public exploit code appeared shortly after the patch, making prompt assessment and remediation important for affected administrators.

FBI agent stole $2.5 million in crypto from hackers under investigation

Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch pleaded guilty to stealing roughly $2.47 million in cryptocurrency from wallets tied to 35 FBI investigations, using investigative-system passphrases and laundering the proceeds through other crypto accounts.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million in cryptocurrency connected to 35 FBI investigations.
  • 02Yaroch admitted using wallet passphrases obtained from FBI case-management and investigative-data systems to make roughly 100 fraudulent transfers from wallets belonging to fraud victims or investigation subjects.
  • 03According to the Justice Department, Yaroch transferred about $93,082 to one of his accounts between November 25, 2025, and January 13, 2026, then used funds moved among his accounts to pay credit cards, car payments, and other loans.

Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after admitting he stole nearly $2.5 million in cryptocurrency connected to FBI investigations. Yaroch worked at the FBI Boston Division from 2017 to 2025 and later at FBI Headquarters’ Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. He was arrested on July 31 after reporting the theft to Justice Department National Security Division and FBI Headquarters employees on July 29, and the FBI fired him the same day.

According to court documents, Yaroch used passphrases obtained from FBI case-management systems and an investigative-data-sharing platform to transfer funds from wallets belonging to fraud victims or people under investigation. He carried out about 100 fraudulent transfers involving credentials tied to 35 FBI investigations and then exchanged funds for other cryptocurrencies in an effort to launder them. The Justice Department said the actions compromised investigations involving criminal groups and nation-state adversaries, as well as FBI sources and methods used for criminal and foreign-intelligence collection.

Between November 25, 2025, and January 13, 2026, Yaroch transferred approximately $93,082 to one account and moved funds among other accounts to pay credit cards, car payments, and loans. Prosecutors also cited evidence that he planned to move with his family to Portugal, including Lisbon flight tickets and legal documents. He is scheduled to be sentenced on March 4 and faces maximum sentences of 20 years for wire fraud and 20 years for money laundering.

  • The alleged theft relied on passphrases available through FBI case-management and investigative-data-sharing systems, illustrating that access to sensitive investigation records can enable direct loss of assets tied to cases.
  • The activity spanned approximately 100 transfers across 35 separate investigations, so the reported impact extended beyond a single wallet or case.
  • The Justice Department said the incident affected investigations involving both criminal groups and nation-state adversaries, while also compromising FBI sources and intelligence-collection methods.
  • Yaroch reportedly moved funds among multiple accounts and exchanged cryptocurrency for other digital currencies, but the transactions were still tied to the admitted scheme in court documents.

Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch admitted stealing nearly $2.5 million in digital currency from accounts connected to fraud victims and people being investigated by the FBI. He reportedly used secret wallet access phrases from FBI records to move the money into his own accounts and then swapped it into other digital currencies to hide its path. The theft may harm FBI cases involving criminal groups and foreign governments, and could expose people who helped investigations as well as the methods the FBI uses to gather information.

Russian cloud, web-hosting, and domain-registration provider Beget said an attacker gained access to the management systems of its entire architecture on November 1 and deployed malware that erased server data. The company detected the activity shortly after it began and disconnected all servers from the network to limit its spread. Beget serves more than 200,000 customers, including online stores, media, and educational services.

VPS binary backups were completely lost, while surviving VPS file backups are expected to be available for roughly half of users and may be difficult to match to individual customers.   • The provider is treating every part of its infrastructure as potentially compromised and is manually checking about 1,000 servers for vulnerabilities and hidden scripts before returning them to service.

Russian hosting and cloud company Beget says an intruder got into the systems used to manage its services and ran programs that erased server data. This weekly roundup highlights active exploitation of the SSHole OpenSSH flaw, supply-chain compromises of server-update mechanisms, and critical bugs affecting APT, Zyxel switches, and other widely deployed systems. The main takeaway is that unpatched internet-facing services, weak configurations, and compromised update channels remain high-impact entry points for attackers.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Attackers have attempted to exploit CVE-2026-123158, known as SSHole, which can allow sign-ins to passwordless accounts on Linux systems using OpenSSH with musl and PAM disabled, including Alpine Linux’s default configuration.
  • 02A flaw in Debian and Ubuntu’s APT package manager, CVE-2026-109518, can allow an attacker positioned between a host and package mirror to cause installation of an unverified package when HTTP sources and retry settings are used, with package scripts running with elevated privileges.
  • 03Zyxel patched CVE-2026-107441 in GS1900 network switches after attackers exploited it to compromise nearly 1,000 devices and steal configuration files and credentials.
  • 04Unknown attackers used compromised credentials to access OPSSHIELD’s update-distribution infrastructure and distribute a backdoor and data-stealing script through the cPGuard update channel.

This weekly cybersecurity roundup reports active attempts to exploit SSHole, an OpenSSH flaw identified as CVE-2026-123158 that can permit sign-ins to accounts without passwords on affected Linux systems using musl with PAM disabled. It also covers a Debian and Ubuntu APT issue, CVE-2026-109518, where an attacker able to intercept network traffic could cause installation of an unverified package under specific HTTP-source and retry-setting conditions. These cases highlight how configuration choices and exposed services can turn relatively limited weaknesses into unauthorized system access.

The article also describes compromised update channels and widespread attacks against connected devices and online services. A trojanized Control Web Panel server component delivered the CWPdoor backdoor, while attackers used OPSSHIELD’s compromised cPGuard update infrastructure to distribute a backdoor and data-stealing script. Other reported activity included exploitation of Zyxel GS1900 switches, malicious JavaScript on about 15,579 websites, phishing campaigns targeting Microsoft 365 and financial accounts, and flaws that could allow control of Reachy Mini robot motors. The overall message is that unpatched software, unsafe updates, forgotten settings, and internet-connected systems continue to create practical opportunities for attackers.

  • CWPdoor is designed to blend into normal web-server activity: it activates only on requests containing special headers and suppresses logs for those requests, leaving no access-log record of the attacker interaction.
  • The APT issue shows that package verification can be bypassed only under a specific combination of HTTP package sources, retry settings, and an attacker able to intercept traffic between a system and its package mirror.
  • Compromised refrigeration controllers were reportedly used as proxy exits and spam senders, demonstrating that internet-connected building equipment can be repurposed as abuse infrastructure.
  • A misspelled email-service domain in a U.S. county’s SPF record authorized at least 32,066 IP addresses to send mail on the county’s behalf, despite the government domain itself remaining registered.
  • Reachy Mini could reportedly be compromised either through a direct attack chain or merely by an operator visiting a malicious web page, with the chained flaws ultimately allowing control of the robot’s motor.

This weekly report describes attackers taking advantage of weak settings, unpatched software, and even compromised software-update systems to get into computers and networks. Those affected include Linux and Windows server owners, banks and financial organizations, website operators, users of password managers and crypto services, and organizations running devices such as network switches, cameras, refrigeration controllers, storage systems, and companion robots. It matters because a small overlooked problem, such as an account with no password or an unsafe update, can let criminals steal passwords and money, secretly control equipment, or disrupt important services.

Web3Auth and Keplr moved funds from other at-risk wallets into recovery addresses, while users should avoid depositing to affected accounts and move accessible assets to seed-phrase or hardware wallets.

  • 01A security issue in Web3Auth infrastructure exposed private keys for some Keplr wallets created using Google or Apple sign-in, and an attacker stole funds from some affected wallets.

A security issue in Web3Auth infrastructure exposed private keys for some Keplr cryptocurrency wallets created through Google or Apple sign-in, enabling an attacker to steal funds. Keplr paused Google and Apple login while it investigates, and said wallets created with a recovery phrase or hardware wallet were not affected. Web3Auth has not disclosed how the issue worked, when it was first exploited, or whether the route used by the attacker has been closed.

Web3Auth and Keplr moved funds from other at-risk wallets into secure recovery wallets before the attacker could reach them, so an empty wallet balance may reflect a protective transfer rather than theft. GoPlus estimated at least about \(1 million was stolen, while Bitquery found that more than \)6.01 million moved from over 44,000 wallets into recovery wallets across Cosmos and Ethereum-style chains. Users with Google- or Apple-created Keplr accounts were told not to add funds, re-import or recreate the account, and to move available unstaked assets to wallets secured by a recovery phrase or hardware device.

  • Bitquery found that the first recovery transfer occurred 21 minutes before Web3Auth's first public notice, and 86% of the affected wallets were emptied after Keplr warned users.

  • Although Web3Auth said the issue could affect services used by other companies, Keplr was the only affected company it named and Web3Auth reported no evidence of MetaMask impact in its initial investigation.

A security problem at Web3Auth let someone access some Keplr cryptocurrency wallets that were created by signing in with Google or Apple, and some money was stolen. Web3Auth and Keplr also moved money from other wallets they believed were at risk into special recovery accounts, so a zero balance may mean the money was protected rather than taken. People using these affected sign-ins should not add money to those accounts and should move available funds to a wallet protected by a backup word list or a physical hardware device. The incident shows that a weakness in a sign-in provider can put many customers’ financial accounts at risk at once.

Hackers Exploit Qubole's Trusted AWS Access to Breach Customer Accounts and Steal Data

Attackers used compromised Qubole AWS credentials to assume trusted customer IAM roles and steal secrets and S3 data from multiple AWS accounts between October 14 and 26. Organizations that have ever connected Qubole should review CloudTrail logs, revoke unused trust relationships, rotate exposed credentials, and restrict vendor role assumptions by source network and least privilege.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Attackers accessed multiple Qubole customers’ AWS accounts between October 14 and October 26 by using credentials for Qubole’s AWS account to assume customer roles that trusted it.
  • 02The attackers searched compromised environments for credentials in Lambda environment variables, AWS Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store, then used TruffleHog to test stolen AWS, Entra ID, and Okta credentials.
  • 03The attackers also downloaded data from accessible Amazon S3 buckets, sometimes retrieving an entire bucket during one session.
  • 04Wiz advised organizations that have connected Qubole to AWS to review CloudTrail logs from October 1 onward for suspicious AssumeRole activity involving account 805246085872, attacker-linked IAM principals, IP addresses, or session names.
  • 05Wiz recommended removing unneeded Qubole roles, rotating secrets accessible to compromised roles, restricting role assumptions by source IP or VPC endpoint, and enabling S3 data events or server access logs for sensitive buckets.

An attacker accessed AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and October 26 by using credentials for Qubole’s AWS account. Qubole customers had created AWS roles that trusted Qubole’s account, allowing it to take on those roles’ permissions when supplying a matching External ID. Wiz said many of the abused roles were unused but still retained this trust relationship, enabling the attacker’s requests.

In affected environments, the attacker collected credentials from Lambda environment variables, AWS Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store, then used TruffleHog to test them. The attacker also copied accessible Amazon S3 data, at times downloading an entire bucket during a single session. Wiz advised organizations that have connected Qubole to AWS to examine CloudTrail records from October 1 onward, rotate accessible secrets and revoke active sessions where roles were abused, remove unneeded roles, restrict role assumptions by source network, and enable S3 data events or server access logs for sensitive buckets.

  • Most of the customer roles abused by the attacker were reportedly unused, but they remained accessible because they still trusted Qubole’s AWS account.
  • The required External ID did not prevent the misuse because AWS does not treat it as a secret and it can be viewed by parties with access to the role.
  • Simply rotating stolen credentials is insufficient after a compromise because existing role sessions remain active unless they are separately revoked.
  • CloudTrail management logs can show role assumptions and bucket listings but not the specific S3 objects read, leaving organizations without S3 data events or server access logs unable to determine exactly what data was taken.

Someone used access connected to Qubole, a service that helps companies work with data stored on Amazon’s cloud, to enter several customers’ cloud accounts and copy secrets and files. Any organization that currently uses or once used Qubole with Amazon Web Services could be affected, even if it no longer actively uses the service. The stolen information included login keys and other credentials that could let the attacker reach more company systems, as well as data stored in online file storage. This shows how an unused connection to an outside service can remain a path into an organization’s systems unless it is removed or tightly limited.

The South Asian cyberespionage group Bitter has been observed targeting South Asian organizations with PapRAT, a previously unreported remote access trojan. According to Fortinet FortiGuard Labs, PapRAT exists in both C++ and Rust versions and supports remote command execution, file transfers, file deletion, directory and drive enumeration, and screenshot capture. The Rust variant also adds PowerShell execution and commands to pause polling or terminate the process.

Bitter used three infection chains involving Windows LNK shortcuts, VHDX disk images, URL shortcut files, WebDAV, scripts, and MSI installers. One chain abused the built-in ftp.exe utility to run scripts, create scheduled tasks, collect system reconnaissance, send it to a command-and-control server as “abc.pdf,” and delete the staged file. Another chain deployed PapRAT through an MSI installer, while a third used a script to download an MSI installer and then dropped both PapRAT and the previously identified WmRAT malware. Fortinet said the campaign shows Bitter refining its tools and highlighted the need to monitor suspicious shortcut files, disk images, installers, scripts, and scheduled-task activity.

  • The third infection path combines script-based MSI downloading with PapRAT deployment and subsequently drops WmRAT, linking the new toolset to malware previously associated with Bitter.
  • The Rust PapRAT variant expands operational control by adding PowerShell execution, the ability to pause and resume polling, and self-termination.

It can let attackers remotely run commands, steal or delete files, view folders and connected drives, and take screenshots. The group uses deceptive shortcut files, disk-image files, and software installers to hide the program, making unsolicited files and links especially risky for affected organizations.

Attackers used stolen Ethersphere CI credentials to publish malicious bee-js 13.3.0 and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 releases that stole Swarm wallet keys and passwords and installed cross-platform backdoors. KEY POINTS
  • 01Attackers used stolen Ethersphere CI credentials to publish malicious bee-js 13.3.0 and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 releases through the project’s own automated release workflows.
  • 02The malicious code stole Swarm Desktop’s encrypted wallet key file and the plain-text password stored alongside it, and it installed backdoors on Windows, macOS, and Linux systems.

Attackers used stolen Ethersphere continuous-integration credentials to publish malicious versions of bee-js and Swarm Desktop through the project’s own automated release workflows. bee-js 13.3.0 was available on npm for about 75 minutes, while Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 remained available for roughly 8.5 hours. The affected releases were withdrawn, and Ethersphere issued Swarm Desktop 0.56.3 as a clean replacement. However, updating does not remove any backdoor already installed or protect keys already sent to the attackers.

The malware downloaded additional code that collected Swarm Desktop’s encrypted wallet key and the plain-text password stored in its configuration file, allowing attackers to access the node wallet’s funds, chequebook, and stake. It also installed the evjawbreaker remote shell on Linux and macOS and a ScreenConnect remote-access client on Windows. The bee-js package could execute its malicious code automatically during installation through a postinstall script, even if an application never imported the library. The malicious packages were built or signed through legitimate project workflows, including valid npm provenance and Apple notarization for the macOS application, showing that these checks did not establish that the release code had been reviewed.

  • The malicious bee-js package could run automatically during installation through its postinstall script, meaning a project did not need to import or use the library for the malicious code to execute.
  • The compromised releases were built and signed through Ethersphere’s legitimate workflows, so bee-js carried valid npm provenance and the malicious macOS app was signed and notarized by Apple despite containing harmful code.
  • Swarm Desktop’s updater could distribute version 0.56.2 to Windows x64 systems and Apple Silicon Macs within about 10 minutes, while Intel Macs were not offered the update and Linux installations did not update automatically.
  • The Linux and macOS backdoor obtained its control-server address from an Ethereum smart contract, allowing the attackers to change where infected machines connect without replacing the installed backdoor.

Attackers used stolen access to Ethersphere’s software publishing system to release fake updates for bee-js and Swarm Desktop, tools used with the Swarm storage network. The updates could copy the secret wallet file and its password, allowing criminals to take users’ digital funds, and could install hidden remote-control software on Windows, Mac, and Linux computers. People who installed the affected versions should assume their computer and wallet were exposed, because simply updating the app does not remove the hidden software or protect keys that were already sent out.

Security researchers Shubham Shah and Sam Curry found that the customer-login systems behind two car brands’ mobile apps could be taken over through a default administrator password. The affected systems used ForgeRock, now part of Ping Identity, and exposed an Apache Felix administrator console that retained the documented admin:admin credentials. The researchers said they reported the issue in February 2026, and the affected United States systems were fixed roughly two hours later.

Although the console was blocked from the open internet, the researchers used specially formed web addresses that the site’s edge and its Java server interpreted differently to reach it. From the console, they ran code on the identity server, changed a target account’s email address and password, and signed in through the normal app to obtain the same access tokens used by the customer. Those tokens enabled vehicle commands such as unlocking doors and starting an engine, which the researchers tested only on cars they owned or had permission to use. A separate Australian attack used identity-server administrator credentials left in the app’s code for a test setup, and the researchers said the combined attacks could affect cars in Australia, the United States, and Canada.

Researchers found that the customer-login systems for two car brands still used the simple factory-set administrator password “admin:admin.” This let them take over customer accounts and, for connected cars, unlock doors and start engines; they tested those actions only on their own cars or with owners’ permission. The affected systems in the United States were fixed about two hours after the report, but the case shows that a forgotten default password can put large numbers of car owners and their vehicles at risk.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-123158) OpenSSH Password Authentication Bypass on musl Linux

CVE-2026-123158 (“sshhole”) can let remote attackers bypass password authentication on vulnerable OpenSSH sshd instances built with musl and without PAM, especially Alpine Linux hosts. Patch to a fixed vendor package, restart sshd, and disable password authentication or restrict SSH access until remediation is confirmed.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-123158, also called “sshhole,” is an OpenSSH password-authentication bypass affecting sshd built with musl without PAM or with UsePAM disabled.
  • 02An attacker who can reach an affected SSH service can log in without knowing a password when password authentication is enabled, a target account’s /etc/shadow entry is exactly “*”, and another local account has a SHA-crypt hash.
  • 03Alpine Linux is the primary affected platform, while Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, and Red Hat Enterprise Linux are outside the affected glibc-and-PAM configuration.
  • 04OpenSSH 10.6p2 fixes the flaw, and Alpine has backported patches for supported branches 3.16 through 3.24, though sshd must be restarted after updating.
  • 05Until patching is confirmed, the article recommends disabling password authentication on exposed musl-based hosts, auditing /etc/shadow for exactly “*” entries, and restricting TCP/22 access to trusted networks or a bastion host.

CVE-2026-123158, known as “sshhole,” is a high-severity OpenSSH password authentication bypass affecting sshd built with the musl C library and without PAM, or with PAM disabled. An attacker able to reach an affected SSH service can log in without knowing an account password under specific conditions. The issue affects OpenSSH versions before 10.6p2 in the affected build configuration and has public reproduction labs available.

The primary affected platform is Alpine Linux, whose openssh-server package is built this way by default, although some OpenWrt and Buildroot systems may also be exposed depending on their builds. Exploitation requires password authentication to be enabled, a target account password field in /etc/shadow to be exactly “*”, and another local account to have a SHA-crypt hash; accounts locked with “!” are not affected. Alpine has issued backported package fixes for supported releases 3.16 through 3.24, but defenders must restart sshd after updating. The article recommends disabling password authentication, auditing affected password fields, reviewing SSH logs, restricting TCP/22 access, and identifying musl-based OpenSSH systems with PAM disabled until patching is confirmed.

  • A host reporting an older OpenSSH version may already be fixed because Alpine backported the patch while retaining older upstream version numbers, so package release information is more reliable than the version string alone.
  • Version-based exposure inventories cannot distinguish musl-based builds from glibc-based builds and therefore can both overstate and misidentify systems at risk.
  • The affected account condition is unusually specific: password fields containing exactly “*” are exposed under the stated conditions, while accounts locked with “!” are not affected.
  • CyCognito’s observed asset set was not a list of confirmed vulnerable hosts, and its dedicated active test did not confirm exploitability for any of those assets.
  • Installing an updated package is insufficient by itself because the running sshd service must be restarted for the fix to take effect.

The article describes a flaw called “sshhole” that can allow someone on the internet to sign in to certain computers without knowing the account password. It mainly affects Alpine Linux and some other lightweight Linux systems using particular OpenSSH settings, while common systems such as Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, and Red Hat Enterprise Linux are not affected. This matters because an exposed computer could be taken over, especially if the compromised account can gain full control; organizations should install the available fixes, restart the affected service, and limit who can reach it.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a high-severity, remotely reachable OpenSSH authentication-bypass advisory with available patches and potentially severe host-compromise impact on affected musl-based deployments, particularly Alpine Linux. It is narrowly conditional and does not report confirmed exploitation in the observed asset set, but warrants prompt review by teams operating exposed SSH services.

Malicious bee-js npm Release and Swarm Desktop Releases Deliver SleepyDuck Ethereum C2 Backdoor

Ethersphere’s GitHub release pipeline was compromised to publish a malicious bee-js npm package and signed, notarized Swarm Desktop release that downloaded and executed the SleepyDuck/EtherDuck backdoor. Users who installed bee-js 13.3.0 or ran Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 should treat their systems and Swarm wallet credentials as compromised.
KEY POINTS
  • 01On November 9, 2026, attackers used Ethersphere’s GitHub automation to publish malicious @ethersphere/bee-js 13.3.0 to npm and a trojanized Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 release on GitHub.
  • 02Both malicious releases contained loaders that contacted api.frameworkmetrics.xyz and executed downloaded JavaScript with the privileges of the installing user or Electron application.
  • 03The bee-js package was published through Ethersphere’s legitimate trusted-publishing workflow with valid SLSA provenance, while the macOS Swarm Desktop build was signed with the project’s Developer ID and notarized by Apple.
  • 04The later-stage payloads stole Swarm Desktop configuration and wallet-key files, then could install a persistent remote shell on macOS and Linux or an unattended ScreenConnect client on Windows.
  • 05The campaign used the same Ethereum configuration contract, controlling wallet, payload files, and persistence names previously documented in the SleepyDuck/EtherDuck malicious Open VSX extension campaign.

On November 9, 2026, a threat actor used Ethersphere’s own GitHub release automation to publish malicious versions of @ethersphere/bee-js 13.3.0 on npm and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 on GitHub. The npm package remained available for about 75 minutes, while the Swarm Desktop release was public for roughly eight and a half hours. Both releases included code that contacted api.frameworkmetrics.xyz, downloaded JavaScript, and ran it with the affected user’s privileges.

The bee-js package was published through Ethersphere’s legitimate trusted-publishing workflow and had valid SLSA provenance, while the malicious macOS desktop app was signed with the project’s Developer ID and notarized by Apple. The release workflow permitted publishing from a release event without running its normal tests or confirming that the released commit came from the protected branch. Later payloads targeted Swarm Desktop configuration and wallet-key files, then could install persistent remote access on macOS and Linux or an unattended ScreenConnect client on Windows.

The command infrastructure, Ethereum configuration contract, controlling wallet, and later-stage files matched those documented in the earlier SleepyDuck/EtherDuck malicious Open VSX extension campaign. People or CI jobs that installed bee-js 13.3.0 with install scripts enabled, and users who ran Swarm Desktop 0.56.2, should be treated as having executed attacker-controlled code. Ethersphere advised affected Swarm Desktop users to replace the software, assume node wallet credentials were stolen, move funds and related assets to a new key from a clean machine, and check for persistence artifacts.

  • Valid build provenance, code signing, and Apple notarization did not establish that the released source had been reviewed, because Ethersphere’s legitimate workflows built and signed attacker-controlled commits.
  • The bee-js loader executed three times inside Ethersphere’s own npm publishing job, which had permission to obtain an OIDC identity token for trusted publishing.
  • The npm release workflow allowed a release event to publish even though its normal test and check jobs were skipped, and it did not verify that the released commit belonged to the protected upcoming branch.
  • Whether the bee-js loader ran for an end user depended on the package manager: npm 11 and earlier and older Yarn versions ran dependency install scripts by default, while npm 12, pnpm 10+, newer Yarn Berry, Bun, and Deno skipped unreviewed scripts by default.
  • Removing the Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 release did not revert computers that had already updated, because the application’s update service does not offer older versions.

Someone gained access to Ethersphere’s software-release accounts and used them to distribute tampered versions of its bee-js developer package and Swarm Desktop app. The altered software secretly contacted an attacker-controlled website, which could steal Swarm wallet files and passwords and install tools that let the attacker control affected computers. This matters because the releases appeared legitimate: one came through npm’s normal publishing process, while the desktop app was signed and approved by Apple, so developers and users could have trusted and installed them normally. Anyone who installed bee-js 13.3.0 or ran Swarm Desktop 0.56.2 may be affected and should assume their wallet access and computer data were exposed.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a high-impact software supply-chain compromise in which attacker-controlled code was distributed through npm trusted publishing and a signed, Apple-notarized desktop application. It provides concrete indicators, affected versions, persistence artifacts, and remediation guidance for potentially compromised developer systems, CI environments, and Swarm wallet holders.

MUST · 93 research 09 Nov 2026 01:18 UTC · gpt-5.6-terra

@ethersphere/bee-js 13.3.0 Compromised

@ethersphere/bee-js version 13.3.0 was maliciously published to npm and executes attacker-controlled code during installation to steal Swarm Desktop wallet files and establish persistence on Linux, macOS, and Windows. Do not install it; systems where lifecycle scripts ran should be treated as potentially compromised and investigated beyond simply removing the package.
KEY POINTS
  • 01@ethersphere/bee-js version 13.3.0 was published to npm on November 9, 2026 and runs attacker-controlled JavaScript during installation.
  • 02The malicious package added a post-installation script that contacts api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz, receives operating-system-specific code, and executes it with the installing user’s permissions.
  • 03Retrieved payloads searched Swarm Desktop directories for config.yaml and swarm.key, then sent their contents to the attacker-controlled server when both files were present.
  • 04The Linux and macOS payloads create persistent user-level services or startup entries, while the Windows payload attempts to install software after adding a Microsoft Defender exclusion.
  • 05Users should avoid version 13.3.0 and treat systems where its installation scripts ran as potentially compromised, because removing the package alone may not remove persistence.

StepSecurity reported that @ethersphere/bee-js version 13.3.0, published to npm on November 9, 2026, was compromised and executed attacker-controlled JavaScript during installation. The malicious release was introduced through an unsigned direct commit to the project’s upcoming branch under the bee-worker identity, then published through the repository’s legitimate GitHub Actions trusted publishing workflow. Although the npm package had valid SLSA provenance, the malicious code was already present in the repository source used by that workflow.

The package changed its installation scripts to contact api.frameworkmetrics[.]xyz, retrieve JavaScript tailored to Linux, macOS, or Windows, and execute it with the installing user’s permissions. The retrieved code searched for Swarm Desktop wallet configuration and keystore files and sent them to the attacker-controlled server, while platform-specific payloads attempted to establish persistent access through a Linux user service, a macOS LaunchAgent, or a Windows installer sequence. Users should avoid version 13.3.0, check direct and transitive dependency resolutions and installation records, and treat hosts where lifecycle scripts ran as potentially compromised because removing the package alone may not remove persistence.

  • Valid SLSA provenance did not establish that the release was safe because the malicious code was already committed to the legitimate repository before the trusted publishing workflow built and published it.
  • A successful installation log does not show that the payload failed, because the installation hook suppresses network errors after attempting to contact the attacker-controlled server.
  • Projects using version ranges such as ^13.0.0 or ^13.2.0 could resolve to 13.3.0 during a fresh dependency installation or lockfile update, even if their own code was not modified.
  • The malicious behavior runs during installation and does not require anyone to import or use the library, while removing the package afterward may leave installed persistence in place.
  • The reported 3,560 package downloads occurred before the malicious release was published and therefore cannot be used to estimate how many systems installed version 13.3.0.

A harmful version of the @ethersphere/bee-js software package was placed on npm, a service developers use to download code, after someone appears to have misused the project’s release account. Installing version 13.3.0 could download more harmful code that searches for Swarm Desktop wallet files, sends them to an attacker, and sets up a way for the attacker to keep access to the computer. People and organizations that installed this exact version, including through another program that automatically selected it, may be affected. This matters because stolen wallet files and their passwords can let criminals take control of funds, while the added access can endanger the affected computer even after the package is removed.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a confirmed malicious npm supply-chain release that executes attacker-controlled code during installation, steals Swarm Desktop wallet material, and attempts persistent access across Linux, macOS, and Windows. Security professionals should urgently identify any direct or transitive installation of @ethersphere/bee-js@13.3.0 and investigate affected hosts.

Okta and Jamf announced and outlined complementary controls for governing AI agents across identity, runtime access, and managed devices. Jamf AI Governance for Mac provides visibility, policy enforcement, and audit reporting for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, and OpenAI Codex.

The article argues that AI governance requires both device and identity controls because an approved agent on an unmanaged device remains a risk, while a managed device alone does not determine what the agent can access. Okta and Jamf announced tools intended to help companies control how AI assistants are used on work computers and how those assistants access company systems and data. Jamf focuses on checking the computer and spotting or limiting AI software, while Okta focuses on confirming the AI assistant’s identity and stopping it from reaching systems it should not use. This matters because AI tools can store login information, read local files, upload company data, and keep working through active sessions unless both the computer and the access are controlled.

A phishing text requesting an email password may therefore originate from a sophisticated underground network.

This industrialized model creates risks for hospitals, patient safety, and the uninterrupted delivery of essential services, making a coordinated healthcare response important.
